narrative: Star Vetter is an automated pipeline that identifies candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite. It starts with over 21,000 target stars, applies statistical filters to light-curve measurements, cross-checks results against six major variable-star catalogs to flag novel objects, and then runs an automated pixel-level contamination check on each one. Candidates that pass this check are listed here with their orbital periods and eclipse depths measured directly from the light curve. The pipeline combines high sensitivity - it catches real signals - with systematic vetting to minimize false alarms. A machine learning model trained on 3,144 labeled examples provides a second opinion on candidate quality, outperforming the rule-based baseline. Because every candidate receives the same rigorous automated scrutiny before listing, and because some carry open caveats noted on their individual pages, the results offer a trustworthy foundation for follow-up study.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such a way that, from Earth's vantage point, one star periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the combined light we receive from the system dips. By measuring these regular dips in brightness over time, astronomers can infer orbital properties like period (how long one orbit takes) and the relative sizes of the two stars.

faqs.question: What does 'candidate' mean here, and how is it different from 'confirmed'?
faqs.answer: A 'candidate' is a target star whose light curve shows a signal consistent with an eclipsing binary, but one that has not yet passed our automated pixel-level check. 'Confirmed' means the candidate passed that check - an automated scan that rules out artifacts caused by nearby bright stars contaminating the measurement. Confirmation here means the signal is on-target and trustworthy; it does not mean the star has received professional follow-up or been added to an official catalog.

faqs.question: What is the ML screening score?
faqs.answer: The screening score is a machine learning model (gradient boosting, trained on 3,144 labeled examples) that predicts whether a candidate is a real eclipsing binary or a false alarm. It outperforms the rule-based pipeline that decides which candidates get checked. The score is a second opinion on candidate quality, not a gate - all candidates that pass the rule-based vetting still receive the automated pixel-level check regardless of the ML score.

faqs.question: How does a candidate get checked?
faqs.answer: Every candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level contamination check. This scan compares the brightness measured at the target's location to brightness in surrounding pixels, looking for signs that the eclipse signal might be caused by a nearby bright star rather than the target itself. The check is fully automated; no human visually inspects each result. Candidates that pass are listed as confirmed.

faqs.question: What if the period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: When a star's brightness is sampled at regular intervals (as TESS does), sometimes an eclipse period can be confused with a different, longer one. To test for this, we compare the depth of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If the depths are significantly different, the period may be aliased. Some candidates carry this caveat on their individual pages, meaning the reported period should be treated with caution.

faqs.question: Can I verify a result myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. TESS light curves are publicly available, and the orbital periods and eclipse depths reported here come directly from those data. If you have the tools and expertise, you can download the light curve for any confirmed candidate and check the measurements yourself.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it is listed here?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the end of this pipeline's work. The site publishes the confirmed candidates and their measured properties (period, eclipse depth) so that the scientific community can find them. What happens next - whether a candidate receives spectroscopic follow-up, is added to a catalog, or becomes part of future studies - is outside the scope of this project.
